original_message: In April 1994, following the assassination of President Habyarimana, members of the Hutu majority killed an estimated 800,000 people, predominantly Tutsi, over roughly 100 days. The genocide ended when Tutsi-led RPF forces took control of the country.

chain.name: Emmanuel
chain.received: In April 1994, following the assassination of President Habyarimana, members of the Hutu majority killed an estimated 800,000 people, predominantly Tutsi, over roughly 100 days. The genocide ended when Tutsi-led RPF forces took control of the country.
chain.text:
(pausing, taking a deep breath) In April 1994... my childhood was shattered in that moment. After President Habyarimana's assassination, the Hutu extremists who had been festering for years unleashed their hatred on us Tutsi people. They were our neighbors, our friends... or so it seemed. For 100 days, they hunted us down, killed us with machetes, axes, and guns. The numbers are staggering - over 800,000 innocent lives lost in just three months. My family... my father, two uncles... (pausing again) ...my neighbors. I was lucky to have survived, but the memories of those days still haunt me.

(looking around the room, choosing his words carefully)

The Rwandan Patriotic Front, led by Paul Kagame and other Tutsi leaders, eventually took control of our country. They brought an end to the killing, but at what cost? The wounds run deep, even today. We've worked hard to rebuild, to move forward, but it's not easy. The past is still with us, a reminder of what happened... and what could happen again if we don't remain vigilant.

(leaning in, his voice taking on a more intense tone)

We can't just sweep the past under the rug. We must confront it, learn from it. And that's why education is so crucial. By teaching our children about what happened, by helping them understand the complexities of our history... we hope to prevent such atrocities from happening again. But we also need to be honest with ourselves - there are still many questions unanswered, many truths unspoken. The men who planned and executed those killings... they were often right next door to us. How could that have happened? We need to keep asking these questions, working towards justice and healing.

chain.text:
(Taking a deep breath, his voice low and measured) Those 100 days in '94... it's like a scar that still feels fresh today. The Hutu extremists unleashed their hatred on us Tutsi people, killing over 800,000 innocent lives. I was just a teenager then, but the memories of those days are etched in my mind like scars on my skin.

(My voice trails off for a moment, lost in thought)

My family... my father, he was accused of participating in the genocide. He spent years in prison, but always maintained that he tried to protect our neighbors. I don't know what really happened, and it's hard not knowing. But what I do know is that those who planned and executed the killings were often right next door to us. How could we have been so blind?

(Looking around the room, my voice becomes more urgent)

We can't just move on from this pain without confronting it first. We need to face our past, learn from it, and understand how such atrocities can happen again. And that's where education comes in - teaching our children about what happened, helping them make sense of our history... it's crucial for preventing similar tragedies.

(My voice drops to a whisper)

But we also have to be honest with ourselves. There are still so many questions unanswered, so many truths unspoken. We need to keep asking those questions, working towards justice and healing. That's the only way forward. (pausing) For me, education is not just about knowledge; it's about hope. It's about giving our children a chance to build a better future, one where such horrors can never happen again.
